intro: Whitetails are browsers: they eat leaves, buds, forbs (broad-leaf weeds), fruit and nuts, and only a little grass. Food drives where deer feed, and the best food changes through the year.
Scout the food that's in season right now, then hunt the cover and trails between it and bedding.
seasons: Green forbs, new leaves and buds, clover, early wheat. Deer chase the green-up on burns, cuts and field edges.
Forbs, soybeans, blackberry and greenbrier leaves, mesquite beans and prickly pear in South Texas.
Persimmons, grapes, beautyberry, and the first white oak acorns. Green plots and wheat start to pull deer.
Acorns (white oaks first, then red), honey locust pods, pecans, food plots, harvested crops.
Red oak acorns that last, green wheat and oats, standing or waste corn and beans, evergreen browse (greenbrier, honeysuckle, yaupon).

intro: In the humid South and East, deer get much of their water from food and dew and rarely need to visit a pond. In dry country (West Texas, the plains, the Southwest), water is a daily draw and a great place to hunt in early season and drought.
On satellite, look for stock tanks, windmills and creeks; in dry country, water within a few hundred yards of thick cover gets daylight visits.
Deer bed where they can see, smell and escape: thick regrowth, the downwind side of ridge points, brushy draws, cattail edges, and tall grass in farm country.
Mature bucks pick the thickest, least-pressured spots and often bed with the wind at their back and a view in front.
Deer move between bedding and food mostly at dawn and dusk, using the easiest route that keeps them hidden: creek bottoms, fencerows, edges, saddles and benches.
Funnels and pinch points (where cover narrows) concentrate movement and are the best stand sites. The Spot finder marks many of these from terrain.
seasons: Predictable bed-to-feed patterns; hunt evening near food from the bedding side.
Bucks make scrapes and rubs along edges and trails; activity increases midday.
Bucks cruise downwind of doe bedding areas and through funnels all day.
Deer go back to food; cold fronts trigger heavy evening feeding.

intro: Deer rely on their nose first. Always hunt with the wind blowing from deer to you; the app's Wind check shows where your scent goes.
Hunting pressure pushes deer into thicker cover and later movement. On public land, the best spots are often the hard-to-reach ones, more than a quarter mile from roads.
seasons: Peaks roughly mid-November in most of the covered states. South Texas and Louisiana are later (December, and as late as January in parts of southeast Louisiana).
Most active the first and last hours of light, more midday during the rut and after cold fronts.

intro: Turkeys are opportunists: acorns and nuts in fall and winter, green leaves and seeds in spring, and insects (grasshoppers, beetles) in summer, which poults depend on.
They scratch leaves aside for mast; fresh scratching (cleared patches in the leaf litter) shows where a flock is feeding.
seasons: Green grass and clover, seeds and insects in open areas, pastures and burns.
Insects in grass, burns and openings; berries.
Acorns, pecans, grapes, waste grain, beautyberry.
Acorns, green wheat and oats, waste grain, chufa.

intro: Turkeys drink daily where water is scarce (Rio Grande and Merriam's range). In wetter country water is rarely the limiting factor.
In dry country, roost trees near water and stock tanks are the core of a flock's range.
Turkeys roost in tall trees, usually on slopes or over water, and spend the day in open woods and fields where they can see danger.
Hens nest in grass and brush in spring; broods need grassy, buggy openings with cover nearby.
A typical day: fly down at first light, strut and feed in openings, move into timber midday, feed again in the afternoon, and fly up to roost at dark.
Turkeys travel ridges, edges and old roads. Find roosts (droppings and feathers under big trees) and work out the route to the strut zone.
Eyesight is their main defense: they see movement and color. Sit still against a wide tree, and use calls sparingly with a wary bird.
In spring, gobblers gobble from the roost, fly down to hens, and strut in open areas. Late morning, after hens go to nest, is often the best time to call in a lonely gobbler.
seasons: Breeding season; gobbling peaks in early to mid spring.
Birds gather in hen-poult flocks and bachelor groups; break up a flock and call them back together.

intro: Mule deer are browsers: they eat the leaves and twigs of shrubs and forbs, and much less grass than elk. What's on the menu changes with the season and elevation.
Find the browse in season, then hunt the slopes and breaks where they bed above it.
seasons: Green-up grass and forbs on low winter range, following the snowmelt uphill.
Forbs and leaves in high basins and aspen.
Oak brush acorns, serviceberry, bitterbrush and mountain mahogany; alfalfa and wheat on the edges of the breaks.
Sagebrush, bitterbrush, mountain mahogany and juniper on low south-facing slopes; green wheat on the plains.

intro: In dry country, water is a daily draw: stock tanks, springs, seeps and wildlife guzzlers. Early season and drought make water the best place to wait.
On satellite, look for tanks and windmills; on topo maps, springs. A water source within a mile of broken bedding cover is ideal.

Mule deer bed where they can see: just below ridgelines, on rims and points, under junipers or pinyons, and in the shade on hot days. They pick north slopes in summer and sunny south slopes in winter.
On the plains they hold in breaks, canyons and brushy draws; in the desert, in washes and on hillsides.
Mountain mule deer migrate: from high summer range down to winter range as the snow piles up, usually starting in late October or November. They follow the same routes every year.
Daily movement is short: feed in the open at night and at first light, then climb to bed by mid-morning.
seasons: Begin moving down with the first heavy snows.
Mid-November into December in most of Colorado and New Mexico; later (December-January) for desert mule deer in Arizona, New Mexico and West Texas.
Low, south-facing slopes, sagebrush and pinyon-juniper.

intro: Spot-and-stalk is the classic method. Glass from a high point at first and last light, find a bedded deer, then plan a stalk that keeps the wind and terrain in your favor.
Spooked mule deer bound off stiff-legged (stotting), then often stop and look back from the next rise. Pressured bucks bed in the steepest, most broken country.
Elk are mostly grazers: grasses and sedges in meadows and parks, plus forbs in summer and browse (aspen, oak brush, mahogany, bitterbrush) in fall and winter.
They eat a lot, so they feed in the open at night and at the edges of the day, then retreat to timber.
seasons: High meadows, grass and forbs, aspen.
Meadows and parks near dark timber; oak brush on the foothills.
Grass on open slopes and parks; alfalfa near the forest edge.
Low winter range: grass, sagebrush and bitterbrush.

intro: Elk drink daily and wallow during the rut. Springs, seeps and wallows on north-facing benches near bedding timber are prime September spots.
In dry Southwest units (Arizona and New Mexico), stock tanks and dirt tanks are where many elk are killed in early season.
Elk bed in dark timber, on north slopes and benches, and in aspen-conifer edges. When pressured, they go to the steepest, thickest timber far from roads, often more than a mile in.
Look for timbered benches and saddles near water and feed.

A typical day: feed in a meadow at night, climb into timber at first light, bed through midday, and move back to feed at dusk. Thermals carry your scent downhill in the morning and uphill in the evening.
Snow pushes elk from high summer range to lower winter range; hunting pressure can push them miles, onto private land or into wilderness.
seasons: Rut: bulls bugle, gather cows and wallow. Herds stay put unless pressured.
Post-rut; bulls go quiet and recover in timber.
Snow starts the migration toward winter range.

intro: The rut runs roughly early September to early October, peaking in the third week of September. Calling (bugles and cow calls) works best then.
Elk have great noses and hearing. Play the thermals, get away from roads, and expect to cover a lot of ground.
Feral hogs eat almost anything: acorns, pecans, crops, roots, grubs, earthworms and carrion. Fresh rooting (turned-up soil, flipped sod) shows where they fed last night.
Follow the season's food: crops in summer, acorns and pecans in fall, rooting in wet bottoms through winter.
seasons: Roots, grubs and green grass; new crops.
Corn, milo, rice and other crops; prickly pear and mesquite beans in South Texas.
Acorns, pecans and persimmons; harvested crops.
Acorns that last, rooting in bottoms and wet ground, green wheat.

intro: Hogs can't sweat, so they need water and mud every day, especially in heat. Wallows by creeks, ponds and sloughs are key sign.
A fresh wallow has cloudy water and wet mud rubbed on nearby trees, knee high.
Hogs bed in groups in the thickest cover around: briars, cutovers, cattails, young pines, swamps and brush. Beds are bowl-shaped depressions, sometimes lined with grass.
Hogs travel creek bottoms, fencelines and field edges between bedding and feeding areas. Where they're pressured, they move almost entirely at night.
Cool, cloudy or rainy days bring more daylight movement.
Hogs have an excellent nose and poor eyesight. Stalk into the wind, slowly, and you can often get close.
Check each area's rules: many WMAs and Corps lakes limit hog hunting to other open seasons, archery only, or a special permit.
Dabbling ducks (mallards, teal, gadwall, pintail, wigeon) feed in shallow water on seeds of moist-soil plants, waste grain (rice, corn, milo) and acorns in flooded timber.
Diving ducks (scaup, canvasbacks, ringnecks) feed in deeper open water on plants and invertebrates.
seasons: Blue-winged teal on shallow mudflats and moist-soil units.
Moist-soil seeds and early flooded fields.
Flooded rice, corn and milo; acorns in green-tree reservoirs.
Birds feed hard before cold fronts and switch to the most reliable food.

intro: Dabblers want shallow water, 6-18 inches, over food. Rain, flooding and drawdowns change where the birds are from week to week, so scout often.
Roost water (big lakes, refuges) and feed water are usually different places; find the route between them.
Hunters need cover too: flooded timber, cattail and reed edges, and brushy shorelines. Birds want calm water out of the wind on blustery days.
Ducks trade between roost and feeding areas at dawn and dusk. Cold fronts from the north push new birds down the flyway.
Big north winds and freezes in the Midwest send waves of mallards into Arkansas, Louisiana and Texas.
Hunt with the wind at your back so birds land into it in front of you. Hide well; ducks see movement and shiny faces.
Many WMAs limit waterfowl hunting to mornings or set days. Tap the area on the map to check its rules.

hardwoods.name: Hardwood forest (oak-hickory)
hardwoods.ground: Broad-leaf trees, mostly oaks and hickories, with an open floor in mature stands. Leaves drop in fall, so winter visibility is long. Look for acorn caps, scrapes along edges and rubs on saplings.
hardwoods.sat: Rounded, puffy crowns in a bumpy, cotton-ball texture. Bright green in summer, gray-brown in leaf-off imagery (winter scenes show the ground through the canopy).

use.deer: Fall feeding when acorns drop; mature open hardwoods are travel cover, not bedding.
use.turkey: Prime fall and winter range: scratching for acorns; big hardwoods are favored roost trees.

pines.name: Pine forest and plantations
pines.ground: Needle-leaf trees. Planted pine stands have trees in straight rows and the same age; thinned stands open up and grow thick brush underneath.
pines.sat: Dark, uniform green year-round. Plantations show straight rows and sharp-edged blocks; thinning lanes appear as parallel stripes.

use.deer: Young (3-8 yr) and recently thinned plantations are thick bedding cover; closed-canopy older pines are poor food.
use.turkey: Open, burned pine stands are good nesting and brood range; closed young pines are avoided.

regrowth.name: Clearcuts and young regrowth
regrowth.ground: Stump-filled openings regrowing in briars, saplings, vines and weeds. Head-high and nearly impenetrable 2-8 years after cutting.
regrowth.sat: Light-colored or brushy patches with straight, sharp edges inside forest. Newer cuts show bare soil and skid trails; older cuts look fuzzy and lighter than the woods around them.

use.deer: Top bedding and browse cover. Edges between a cut and mature timber are classic stand sites.
use.turkey: Fresh cuts are brood and bugging areas; once too thick, turkeys skirt the edges.
use.hog: Thick cutovers are favored bedding.

brush.name: Brush and shrubland
brush.ground: Waist- to head-high woody shrubs and small trees: plum thickets, sumac, mesquite, buckbrush or oak shinnery depending on the region.
brush.sat: Speckled, grainy texture of small dark dots on lighter ground. Denser brush reads darker.

use.deer: Bedding and escape cover, especially in open country where it's the only cover.
use.turkey: Loafing and escape cover; plum and sumac thickets near open ground get used.
use.mule: Bedding cover in draws and breaks.
use.hog: Bedding cover in brush country.

cedar.name: Cedar (juniper) thickets
cedar.ground: Dense evergreen juniper, often taking over old pastures. Red cedar in the east, Ashe juniper in the Texas Hill Country, one-seed and Utah juniper in the West.
cedar.sat: Dark green dots or blobs scattered over pasture, merging into solid dark patches as they fill in. Stays dark green in winter when everything else is brown.

use.deer: Winter thermal cover and bedding; little food value.
use.turkey: Roosting where big trees are scarce; dense cedar is poor turkey habitat.
use.mule: Bedding in juniper breaks and canyon rims; winter cover.

bottoms.name: Creek and river bottoms
bottoms.ground: Strips of big hardwoods (pecan, elm, hackberry, sycamore, cottonwood) along creeks, with vines and thick understory.
bottoms.sat: Winding, darker green ribbons following drainages across open country. Look for the stream line in the middle and the tree band along it.

use.deer: Natural travel corridors linking bedding and food; crossings, inside bends and narrow spots funnel movement.
use.turkey: Main roosting habitat in prairie and brush country: big trees along water. Birds fly down to adjacent fields.
use.hog: Main travel routes and feeding areas; rooting under oaks and pecans.
use.duck: Backwaters and sloughs in flooded bottoms hold wood ducks and mallards.

swamp.name: Bottomland hardwoods and swamps
swamp.ground: Flood-prone forest of overcup, willow and water oaks, cypress and tupelo, with sloughs and standing water in winter.
swamp.sat: Dark forest with irregular water channels and oxbows. Flooded timber appears dark with mirror-like water showing through.

use.deer: Islands of high ground and thickets inside swamps are pressure refuges.
use.turkey: Good on higher ridges between sloughs; birds leave flooded areas.
use.duck: Flooded timber is prime mallard and wood duck habitat in winter.
use.hog: Bedding and wallowing in the wettest, thickest cover.

marsh.name: Marsh and emergent wetlands
marsh.ground: Open wetland with cattails, bulrush, smartweed and sedges in shallow water.
marsh.sat: Mottled green and dark water patches with no trees. Open water is black or dark blue; vegetation is lighter green or tan.

use.duck: Feeding and resting habitat; shallow, seed-producing marsh (smartweed, millet) draws dabblers.
use.deer: Cattail and reed edges are bedding cover in farm country.
use.hog: Cattails and reeds are bedding cover; they root in the mud.

grass.name: Native grass, prairie and CRP
grass.ground: Tall grasses such as switchgrass, bluestem and Indiangrass, often with forbs. CRP fields are retired cropland planted to grass.
grass.sat: Smooth, even texture, tan in fall and winter. CRP fields have straight field edges but no crop rows or pivot circles.

use.deer: Tall grass is bedding cover in farm and prairie country, especially for mature bucks.
use.turkey: Nesting cover in spring; brood range for bugs in summer.

pasture.name: Pasture and hayfields
pasture.ground: Short, grazed or mowed grass with cattle, ponds and fencelines.
pasture.sat: Smooth light green with stock ponds, cattle trails and hay bale dots. Mowed fields show striped patterns.

use.deer: Night feeding and green-up in spring and fall; edges with timber get daylight use.
use.turkey: Strutting and feeding areas; spring gobblers display in open pastures.
use.elk: Grassy openings and parks are night feeding areas.

crops.name: Crop fields
crops.ground: Row crops (corn, soybeans, milo, cotton) or small grains (wheat, oats).
crops.sat: Geometric fields with visible rows; center-pivot circles in the plains. Color changes with the crop stage and harvest.

use.deer: Major food source. Standing corn and beans are also cover until harvest.
use.turkey: Waste grain after harvest is fall and winter food.
use.duck: Flooded or harvested grain fields draw feeding mallards and geese.

burn.name: Recent burns
burn.ground: Blackened ground and scorched trunks for a few months, then a flush of tender green forbs and sprouts.
burn.sat: Dark charred patch with sharp edges right after the fire, then brighter green than its surroundings the next growing season.

use.deer: New growth 1-3 years after a burn is high-quality browse.
use.turkey: Burned areas are bugging and strutting grounds; turkeys find seeds and insects easily.

foodplot.name: Wildlife openings and food plots
foodplot.ground: Small planted openings (clover, wheat, oats, brassicas) inside timber, common on WMAs and leased ground.
foodplot.sat: Small, bright green rectangles or odd-shaped openings inside forest, often along roads or pipelines.

use.deer: Evening feeding destinations; trails enter from the thickest cover side.
use.turkey: Spring strut zones and summer bug fields.

edges.name: Edges and transitions
edges.ground: Where two cover types meet: timber to field, pines to hardwoods, thick to open.
edges.sat: Any line where texture or color changes. Inside corners (where an edge turns) and points of timber into fields stand out.

use.deer: Most daylight deer movement follows edges; inside corners and points are classic stand sites.
use.turkey: Turkeys travel and feed along edges, then step into openings.
use.hog: Hogs travel field edges and fencelines at night.
use.mule: Feed along the edges of fields, burns and openings at first and last light.

terrain.name: Terrain funnels: saddles, benches, ridges
terrain.ground: Low gaps between hilltops (saddles), flat shelves on slopes (benches), and ridge points.
terrain.sat: Easier to see on the Topo or Terrain basemap: saddles are dips in a ridgeline, benches are wide spacing between contour lines.

use.deer: Bucks cross ridges at saddles and travel benches just below the crest; points are bedding spots.
use.turkey: Turkeys strut and roost along ridges and use benches to travel.
use.mule: Bed just under ridgelines and rims with a view; glass the opposite slope.
use.elk: Elk cross ridges at saddles and bed on benches on north slopes.

water_pond.name: Ponds, tanks and water holes
water_pond.ground: Stock ponds, earthen tanks, guzzlers and springs. Look for tracks along the muddy edge.
water_pond.sat: Small dark blue or brown dots and teardrops, often with a dam on the downhill side. Dry-country water shows as a green ring.

use.deer: Daily water in dry weather and in the West; tanks near cover get used in daylight.
use.turkey: Turkeys water daily in dry country; tanks near roost trees are hot spots.
use.elk: Critical in dry country; wallows near water in the rut.
use.mule: Tanks, springs and guzzlers are early-season hot spots in dry country.
use.hog: Daily water and wallows, especially in hot weather.
use.duck: Stock tanks and small ponds hold teal, gadwall and wood ducks, especially on cold mornings.

whiteoak.name: White oak acorns
whiteoak.ground: Rounded leaf lobes with no bristle tips; light gray, scaly bark. Acorns sprout in fall and are sweeter (lower tannin), so deer eat them first.
whiteoak.sat: Inside hardwood forest. Can't be told from other oaks on satellite; scout the ground.

use.deer: Top fall food. Find the white oaks dropping now and you find the deer.
use.turkey: Major fall and winter food.
use.hog: Hogs follow the acorn drop.

redoak.name: Red oak acorns (red, water, willow, post)
redoak.ground: Pointed, bristle-tipped leaf lobes. Acorns take two years to mature and are bitter, so they last into winter.

use.deer: Late-season food after white oak acorns are gone.
use.turkey: Winter staple.
use.duck: Pin oak and willow oak acorns feed mallards and wood ducks in flooded timber.
use.hog: Red oak acorns carry hogs through winter.

honeylocust.name: Honey locust pods
honeylocust.ground: Tree with large branched thorns and long, twisted brown pods in fall and winter.
honeylocust.sat: Often scattered in pastures and fencerows.

use.deer: Sweet pods are eaten fall through winter.

persimmon.name: Persimmon
persimmon.ground: Small tree with blocky, alligator-hide bark; orange fruit ripens after the first frosts.

use.deer: Deer hit dropping fruit hard in October and November.
use.turkey: Eaten when on the ground.
use.hog: Hogs eat fallen fruit in fall.

greenbrier.name: Greenbrier
greenbrier.ground: Thorny green vine with heart-shaped, glossy leaves, forming tangles. Leaves often stay green into winter.
greenbrier.sat: Part of thick understory; not visible from above.

use.deer: Key browse in winter and early spring, especially in the South.

honeysuckle.name: Japanese honeysuckle
honeysuckle.ground: Twining vine with paired oval leaves that stay green most of winter; white-yellow flowers in spring.
honeysuckle.sat: Along edges and in thinned or cut timber.

use.deer: Winter browse staple where it grows.

yaupon.name: Yaupon holly
yaupon.ground: Evergreen shrub with small, scalloped leaves and red berries; forms dense thickets under pines and hardwoods.
yaupon.sat: Understory; makes forest look darker in winter imagery.

use.deer: Year-round browse and bedding cover in East Texas and Louisiana.

beautyberry.name: American beautyberry
beautyberry.ground: Shrub with clusters of bright purple berries hugging the stem in late summer and fall.

use.deer: Leaves are summer browse.
use.turkey: Berries eaten in fall.

mesquite.name: Honey mesquite beans
mesquite.ground: Thorny small tree with feathery leaves and long yellowish bean pods in summer.
mesquite.sat: Speckled brush pattern in South and West Texas.

use.deer: Summer protein-rich beans.
use.turkey: Mesquite flats are Rio Grande turkey range.
use.hog: Hogs eat fallen beans.

pricklypear.name: Prickly pear cactus
pricklypear.ground: Flat, spiny cactus pads with purple-red fruit (tunas) in late summer.
pricklypear.sat: Not visible; grows in brushland and dry pasture.

use.deer: Fruit in summer and pads in drought are important water and food in South Texas.
use.hog: Fruit eaten.

forbs.name: Forbs (weeds): ragweed, sunflower, partridge pea
forbs.ground: Broad-leaf weeds in disturbed ground, burns, fallow fields and road edges.
forbs.sat: Fallow and recently disturbed openings; burns.

use.deer: High-protein spring and summer food; deer prefer forbs over grass.
use.turkey: Seeds and the insects on them feed poults and adults.
use.mule: Summer's main food; green-up after rain draws them out.

wheat.name: Winter wheat and oats
wheat.ground: Green, grass-like fields planted in fall that stay green all winter.
wheat.sat: Bright green fields in late fall and winter when everything else is brown.

use.deer: Prime late-fall and winter green forage in the plains.
use.turkey: Winter flocks feed in green wheat.
use.mule: Plains mule deer feed in green wheat in late fall and winter.
use.hog: Hogs graze and root in green wheat.

corn.name: Corn and milo
corn.ground: Tall row crops; harvested fields leave waste grain.
corn.sat: Rows and pivot circles; tan after harvest.

use.deer: High-energy food in late fall and winter.
use.turkey: Waste grain in winter.
use.duck: Mallards and geese feed in harvested corn.
use.hog: Hogs raid standing and harvested corn.

soybeans.name: Soybeans
soybeans.ground: Low bushy row crop; green in summer, yellow to brown in fall before harvest.
soybeans.sat: Fields turn yellow in early fall, then brown.

use.deer: Green leaves in summer; pods in late fall and winter.

clover.name: Clover and food-plot greens
clover.ground: Low three-leaf plants in planted plots, pipelines and pasture edges.

use.deer: Spring and fall green forage.
use.turkey: Turkeys pick clover and the bugs in it.

blackberry.name: Blackberry and dewberry
blackberry.ground: Thorny canes in old fields, cuts and edges; berries in late spring and early summer.
blackberry.sat: Part of brushy openings and regrowth.

use.deer: Leaves are browse year-round.
use.turkey: Berries eaten in summer.

grape.name: Wild grape
grape.ground: Woody vines climbing into trees, shredding bark, clusters of small dark grapes in late summer.

use.deer: Fruit and leaves eaten.
use.turkey: Fruit eaten into fall.

pecan.name: Pecan
pecan.ground: Tall hickory with compound leaves along rivers; nuts fall in October and November.
pecan.sat: Big crowns along rivers and in orchards.

use.deer: Fallen nuts eaten in fall.
use.turkey: Important fall food in river bottoms.
use.hog: Hogs root for nuts.

chufa.name: Chufa and insects
chufa.ground: Grass-like sedge with underground tubers, planted for turkeys; insects are found in grass and burns.

use.turkey: Turkeys scratch up chufa tubers in winter; spring and summer diet is heavy on insects.

oakbrush.name: Gambel oak (oak brush)
oakbrush.ground: Shrubby oak in dense stands on foothill slopes; acorns in fall.
oakbrush.sat: Mottled dark patches on south and west slopes below the conifers.

use.deer: Mule deer fall food and cover.
use.turkey: Merriam's turkeys eat the acorns.
use.mule: Fall food (acorns and leaves) and cover on foothill slopes.

ponderosa.name: Ponderosa pine forest
ponderosa.ground: Tall pines with orange, puzzle-piece bark and open grassy floors.
ponderosa.sat: Dark dots spaced on lighter grassy ground at mid elevations.

use.turkey: Core Merriam's turkey habitat; big pines are roost trees.
use.deer: Mule deer summer and fall range.
use.mule: Summer and fall range on the mid slopes.

sagebrush.name: Sagebrush
sagebrush.ground: Gray-green aromatic shrub covering open basins and foothills.
sagebrush.sat: Even gray-green speckled texture across broad flats.

use.deer: Mule deer winter range and food.
use.mule: Winter food and range; deer feed on sage when snow covers everything else.

aspen.name: Aspen stands
aspen.ground: White-barked trees in clones, golden in fall, often with lush grass and forbs underneath.
aspen.sat: Bright green patches among dark conifers in summer, yellow in fall imagery.

use.elk: Summer and fall feeding and bedding; aspen-conifer edges are hot spots.
use.deer: Mule deer summer range.
use.mule: Summer range; aspen-conifer edges hold bucks in early season.

sprucefir.name: Dark timber (spruce-fir)
sprucefir.ground: Dense, dark forest of Engelmann spruce and subalpine fir, mostly on north slopes and high benches. Cool, shady and full of blowdown; elk beds are oval patches of flattened needles.
sprucefir.sat: The darkest, finest-textured green on the mountain, mostly on north-facing slopes. Aspen stands and meadows show as lighter patches inside it.

use.elk: Midday bedding and escape cover, especially for pressured elk. Benches and saddles in dark timber near water are prime.
use.mule: Big bucks summer near timberline and bed on timber edges with a view.

meadow.name: Mountain meadows and parks
meadow.ground: Grassy openings in the forest, wetter and greener along the drainages, with sedges and forbs.
meadow.sat: Light green to tan openings ringed by dark timber; wet meadows look brighter along the stream.

use.elk: Night and first- and last-light feeding. Glass the timber edges at dawn and dusk.

wallow.name: Springs, seeps and wallows
wallow.ground: Wet, muddy spots at springs and seeps, often on benches. Fresh wallows have cloudy water, tracks, and mud rubbed on nearby trees; elk wallows smell strongly of urine in the rut.
wallow.sat: Hard to see directly. Look for small bright-green spots or a line of greener trees on a bench below a spring; topo maps mark springs.

use.elk: Bulls wallow daily in September. A fresh wallow near bedding timber is a top ambush site.
use.hog: Hogs need mud to cool off. Fresh wallows mean they're bedding close by.
use.deer: Seeps stay green and draw deer in dry spells.
use.mule: Springs and seeps are daily water in dry country.

bitterbrush.name: Antelope bitterbrush
bitterbrush.ground: Gray-green shrub, 2-6 ft, with small three-lobed leaves; grows with sagebrush on foothills.
bitterbrush.sat: Looks like sagebrush from above. Look for shrub-covered south and west slopes in the foothills.

use.mule: Top fall and winter browse. Heavily clipped (hedged) plants mean deer winter here.

mahogany.name: Mountain mahogany
mahogany.ground: Shrub with small, toothed, leathery leaves and feathery, corkscrew-tailed seeds; on rocky slopes and ridges.
mahogany.sat: Dark, clumpy shrubs on rocky slopes and rims, between the oak brush and the pinyon-juniper.

use.mule: Prime browse fall through winter; bucks bed on rocky points nearby.

pinyon.name: Pinyon-juniper woodland
pinyon.ground: Short, bushy pinyon pines and junipers spaced over rocky ground. Pinyon nuts drop in fall in good years.
pinyon.sat: Evenly spaced dark dots on tan or reddish ground across mesas and foothills.

use.mule: Core winter range: shelter from wind and snow, with browse in the openings.
use.turkey: Merriam's turkeys feed on pinyon nut crops.

alfalfa.name: Alfalfa fields
alfalfa.ground: Low, dense, bright green hay crop with three-part leaves and purple flowers; cut several times a year.
alfalfa.sat: Bright green fields (center-pivot circles in the West) that stay green when pasture is brown.

use.deer: Late summer through fall, and on mild winter days.
use.mule: Valley and plains mule deer feed in alfalfa at night.
use.elk: Elk raid alfalfa at night; you can hunt them only where it borders public land.

playa.name: Playa lakes
playa.ground: Shallow, round, rain-filled basins on the flat High Plains; dry much of the year, flooded after big rains.
playa.sat: Round or oval darker spots in cropland and grass, with green rings or open water when wet.

use.duck: Wet playas hold huge numbers of ducks in fall and winter.
use.deer: Water and weedy cover on the open plains.

moistsoil.name: Moist-soil plants (wild millet, smartweed)
moistsoil.ground: Seedy annual grasses and weeds that sprout on mudflats as water drops in summer: barnyard grass (wild millet), smartweed, sedges. Heavy seed heads by fall.
moistsoil.sat: Green-to-tan flats inside managed wetland units and lake edges, often split into cells by straight or curving levees.

use.duck: Top food for dabblers when flooded 6-18 inches deep; the core of most WMA waterfowl units.

greentree.name: Flooded timber (green-tree reservoirs)
greentree.ground: Bottomland oaks flooded shallow in winter, behind levees or by rivers. Mallards drop through holes in the canopy to feed on acorns.
greentree.sat: Dark bottomland forest with straight levee lines and water-control structures along it. Winter imagery may show water under bare trees.

use.duck: Classic mallard hunting: pin oak, willow oak and Nuttall oak acorns plus cover. Hunt the holes in the canopy.
use.deer: Dry ridges inside flooded timber concentrate deer.
use.hog: Hogs follow the acorn drop on the ridges.

rice.name: Rice fields
rice.ground: Flat fields with low, curving levees. After harvest, stubble and waste grain, often flooded in winter.
rice.sat: Flat fields cut by thin curving levee lines that follow the contour.

use.duck: Flooded harvested rice is prime duck and goose food; birds trade between it and roost water.
use.hog: Hogs raid rice field edges.

beaver.name: Beaver ponds and sloughs
beaver.ground: Creeks backed up behind stick-and-mud dams, with standing dead timber and flooded brush.
beaver.sat: Small, irregular water in creek bottoms, often ringed by gray dead trees.

use.duck: Wood ducks and mallards, especially on public land with little other water.
use.deer: Crossings at the dams and browse along the edges.
use.hog: Hogs wallow and root along the edges.

milo.name: Grain sorghum (milo)
milo.ground: Corn-like plants with a dense, round red or tan seed head on top; stands into fall.
milo.sat: Crop fields, reddish-brown when ripe; hard to tell from other crops on most imagery.

use.deer: Fall food on the plains; standing milo is also cover.
use.hog: Hogs hit milo hard.

Edwards Plateau.note: Hill Country of limestone hills, live oak, Ashe juniper (cedar) and shin oak. Very high deer numbers and small-bodied deer. Rio Grande turkeys roost in pecans and big oaks along creeks.
Edwards Plateau.deer: Acorns (live oak, shin oak, Spanish oak), forbs after rain, and browse; cedar breaks and draws are bedding cover.
Edwards Plateau.turkey: Roosts along creek bottoms; birds feed in openings and pastures nearby.
Edwards Plateau.hog: Hogs along creeks and river bottoms.

Southern Texas Plains.note: South Texas brush country: mesquite, blackbrush, prickly pear, granjeno. Famous for big-antlered deer; rut runs late (December into January).
Southern Texas Plains.deer: Forbs after rain, mesquite beans in summer, prickly pear, and brush browse. Water is a major draw.
Southern Texas Plains.turkey: Rio Grande turkeys roost in big mesquites and along creeks; water holes are key.
Southern Texas Plains.hog: High hog numbers in the brush; water holes and feeders draw them.

Cross Timbers.note: A patchwork of post oak and blackjack oak woods mixed with prairie and pasture. Deer and Rio Grande turkeys use oak mottes and creek bottoms next to open ground.
Cross Timbers.deer: Post oak and blackjack acorns, forbs, wheat fields; creek bottoms and cedar are cover.
Cross Timbers.turkey: Roosts along creeks; feeds in pastures and wheat.
Cross Timbers.hog: Hogs in creek bottoms and oak mottes.

East Central Texas Plains.note: Post Oak Savannah: post oak woods, yaupon thickets and pasture on sandy soils.
East Central Texas Plains.deer: Post oak acorns, yaupon, greenbrier, forbs; yaupon and creek bottoms are bedding cover.
East Central Texas Plains.turkey: Eastern-Rio Grande mix; creek bottoms with big trees.
East Central Texas Plains.hog: Hogs root the post oak bottoms and creek banks; wallows along creeks and stock ponds.

Texas Blackland Prairies.note: Mostly farmed prairie with little public land; cover is limited to creek bottoms, fencerows and Corps lake lands.
Texas Blackland Prairies.deer: Crops, wheat and forbs; bottoms and brushy draws are the cover.

South Central Plains.note: Piney Woods: loblolly and shortleaf pine plantations, hardwood bottoms and clearcuts on national forests and timber lands.
South Central Plains.deer: Browse (greenbrier, yaupon, honeysuckle, beautyberry), acorns in the bottoms, food plots on WMAs. Thinned and cut timber is the best food and cover.
South Central Plains.turkey: Eastern turkeys in mature pine-hardwood with burns; bottoms for roosting.
South Central Plains.hog: Hogs in creek bottoms, cutovers and young pines.
South Central Plains.duck: Wood ducks on beaver ponds and creeks; flooded timber on the bigger rivers.

Western Gulf Coastal Plain.note: Coastal prairie and marsh, rice country and bottomland along the coast; waterfowl country.
Western Gulf Coastal Plain.deer: Bottoms, brushy fencerows and marsh edges.
Western Gulf Coastal Plain.duck: Coastal marsh and rice country: the Texas and Louisiana duck capital.
Western Gulf Coastal Plain.hog: Hogs in rice country and coastal bottoms.

Mississippi Alluvial Plain.note: The Delta: bottomland hardwoods, cypress-tupelo swamps and big ag fields. World-class waterfowl and big-bodied deer.
Mississippi Alluvial Plain.deer: Acorns (overcup, nuttall, water oak), soybeans and corn; high ground in the swamp is refuge during floods.
Mississippi Alluvial Plain.duck: The heart of the flyway: flooded rice and green-tree reservoirs for mallards.
Mississippi Alluvial Plain.hog: Hogs in the bottomland ridges and crop edges.

Ouachita Mountains.note: East-west ridges of pine and oak, much of it Ouachita National Forest.
Ouachita Mountains.deer: Acorns on ridges and benches, browse in cuts and burns; saddles funnel movement.

Arkansas Valley.note: Valley of farms and pasture between the Ozarks and Ouachitas, with river bottoms and Corps lakes.
Arkansas Valley.deer: Crops, pasture edges, acorns in wooded hills.

Boston Mountains.note: Steep, deeply cut oak-hickory plateau (Ozark National Forest).
Boston Mountains.deer: Acorns, benches and hollows; low deer density on big timber.
Boston Mountains.turkey: Ridges and benches in mature hardwoods.

Ozark Highlands.note: Oak-hickory forest with glades, pine in the south, clear rivers; lots of MDC conservation areas and Mark Twain National Forest.
Ozark Highlands.deer: Acorns dominate fall; glades, cuts and old fields for browse.
Ozark Highlands.turkey: Prime Eastern turkey range: hardwood ridges and openings.

Central Irregular Plains.note: Rolling farmland and pasture with wooded draws and river bottoms.
Central Irregular Plains.deer: Crops and wooded edges; draws and CRP are bedding cover.
Central Irregular Plains.turkey: Woodlots and bottoms next to fields.

Interior River Valleys and Hills.note: Big river bottoms and wooded bluffs along the Missouri and Mississippi rivers.
Interior River Valleys and Hills.deer: Crops in the bottoms, acorns on the bluffs.

Western Corn Belt Plains.note: Intensive corn and soybean farming with small woodlots and draws.
Western Corn Belt Plains.deer: Corn and beans; any timber, CRP or cattails is cover.

Flint Hills.note: The largest tallgrass prairie left, grazed and burned each spring; wooded creeks.
Flint Hills.turkey: Creek-bottom roosts, burned prairie for strutting and bugs.

Central Great Plains.note: Mixed-grass prairie and wheat country with river breaks and shelterbelts.
Central Great Plains.deer: Wheat, milo, alfalfa; river bottoms, plum thickets and CRP.
Central Great Plains.turkey: Rio Grande turkeys roost in cottonwoods along rivers.

High Plains.note: Flat shortgrass and irrigated cropland; playa lakes.
High Plains.deer: Crops and CRP; cover is scarce, so any draw or shelterbelt holds deer. Mule deer in the breaks.
High Plains.mule: Mule deer in the breaks and draws.
High Plains.duck: Playa lakes fill after rains and hold huge numbers of ducks.

Southwestern Tablelands.note: Canyons, breaks and mesas with cedar, mesquite and shinnery oak.
Southwestern Tablelands.deer: Mule deer in the breaks, whitetails along rivers; shinnery oak and mesquite.
Southwestern Tablelands.turkey: Rio Grande turkeys along rivers and canyons.
Southwestern Tablelands.mule: Mule deer in the breaks and canyons; glass from the rims.

Chihuahuan Desert.note: Desert grassland and shrubland; water is everything.
Chihuahuan Desert.deer: Desert mule deer; browse and water.
Chihuahuan Desert.mule: Desert mule deer; rut in December-January; hunt water and glass hillsides.

Arizona/New Mexico Mountains.note: Ponderosa pine and mixed conifer mountains (Mogollon Rim, Gila); elk, Merriam's and Gould's turkeys, Coues and mule deer.
Arizona/New Mexico Mountains.deer: Mule deer and Coues whitetail in oak and pine.
Arizona/New Mexico Mountains.turkey: Merriam's turkeys in ponderosa pine; roost in big pines.
Arizona/New Mexico Mountains.mule: Mule deer in the oak and pine; Coues whitetail in the oaks.
Arizona/New Mexico Mountains.elk: Big-bodied elk in ponderosa and mixed conifer; stock tanks are key in dry falls.

Arizona/New Mexico Plateau.note: High plateaus of pinyon-juniper, sagebrush and grassland.
Arizona/New Mexico Plateau.deer: Mule deer in pinyon-juniper and sage.
Arizona/New Mexico Plateau.mule: Pinyon-juniper and sage with water the limiting factor.
Arizona/New Mexico Plateau.elk: Elk on the forested edges and in pinyon-juniper in winter.

Southern Rockies.note: High mountains: aspen, spruce-fir, oak brush foothills; the heart of Colorado elk country.
Southern Rockies.deer: Mule deer migrate between high summer and low winter range.
Southern Rockies.turkey: Merriam's turkeys in ponderosa and oak brush foothills.
Southern Rockies.mule: Classic migrators: high basins in summer, sagebrush and pinyon on winter range.
Southern Rockies.elk: The heart of Colorado elk country: dark timber, aspen and meadows; the September rut in the high country.

Colorado Plateaus.note: Canyons and mesas with pinyon-juniper and sage.
Colorado Plateaus.mule: Canyon and mesa country; important winter range.
Colorado Plateaus.elk: Winter range in pinyon-juniper and sage.

Sonoran Desert.deer: Desert mule deer in washes; water.

Madrean Archipelago.note: Sky islands: desert grassland up to oak and pine; Coues whitetail country.
Madrean Archipelago.deer: Coues deer in oak woodland; glass hillsides.

Interior Plateau.note: Rolling hills of oak-hickory and farms.
